newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Ringgit surges vs dollar as funds bail out.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ringgit surges vs dollar as funds bail out.

text.p: The ringgit strengthened further on Thursday as offshore players sold the U.S. dollar amid signs that Malaysian authorities were determined to defend their currency from speculative attacks, dealers said.
U.S. investment houses unwound their long dollar/ringgit positions, they said.
At 0930 GMT, the ringgit was at 2.4900/10 to a dollar, after firming to 2.4870/80, its strongest level since May 19. It closed at 2.5033/43 in Kuala Lumpur on Wednesday.
"Some big U.S. investment houses were unwinding," said Ishak Ismail, market analyst with research house I.D.E.A.
"The overnight price action was to buy at 2.50, but once the market continued selling (dollars) actively at that level, the plan seems to have been dropped," he said.
He said the ringgit's fall below 2.4980 and then 2.4950 triggered heavy stop-loss sales of the dollar.
Dealers said players, fearing the central Bank Negara would re-impose capital controls to broaden its intervention tools, were also scrambling for the ringgit in the spot market.

Dealers said there was talk that the authorities were asking local banks to reveal the extent of their involvement in the forward market and advising them to be extremely cautious in offering forward contracts in ringgit to offshore players.
Bank Negara governor Ahmad Mohamed Don on Wednesday warned of tough steps, including increasing interest rates, to stamp out speculation in the ringgit.
In a rare public statement, Ahmad said that Malaysia would use all means possible to defend its currency, which has been under pressure from overseas selling in the wake of a crisis in the Thai baht.
On Tuesday, Bank Negara intervened to bolster the ringgit, selling an estimated $1.0 billion.

Malaysian Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Thursday that the country's stability and its strong economic fundamentals should not provide any reason for the ringgit's strength to be undermined.
He added that the central bank would take whatever measures necessary to fend off speculators in the currency market.
Analysts said that the current situation does not warrant the introduction of capital controls, although some did not rule out that possibility.
"Malaysia has done that before, and I wouldn't rule it out," Bernhard Eschweiler, head of economic research (Asia) at J.P. Morgan, told Reuters Financial Television.

"However, there has been a price associated with capital controls in Malaysia. They experienced capital outflow for almost two years in 1994 and 1995. It would have to go very far before the government would consider re-introducing the capital controls," he said.

In 1994, faced with a strong flow of hot money into the country, Bank Negara imposed negative interest rates on foreign deposits, banned swaps and stopped foreigners from buying Malaysian government paper.
Ishak of I.D.E.A. said the ringgit was expected to trade to 2.4750 a dollar in the near term.
"Dollar should be capped around 2.4920/30," he said.
John Noonan, head of international sales/proprietary trading at National Australia Bank in Singapore, said he believed 2.49-2.50 was fair value for the ringgit.

"I think Malaysia has taken some flak (due) to the instability of the region. The region's credibility was damaged with what happened, but I don't think that the fundamentals apply to Malaysia," he said, referring to the Thailand's economic woes.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
